opus-5.5.text:
Around that time, my sense was that the field was at a real turning point. Pre-training had been the dominant paradigm for years: you scale up data and compute, and capabilities keep improving. But by mid-2024 many people were starting to feel that this curve alone wouldn't be enough. High-quality data is finite, and simply making the model bigger was giving diminishing returns on the things we cared about most, like long-horizon reasoning, coding, and acting as an agent.

Reinforcement learning looked like the natural next lever. In pre-training, the model imitates. In RL, the model can actually try things, get feedback, and improve beyond what's in the data. Once you have a strong enough base model, RL stops being a fragile research toy and starts to actually work at scale. That was the shift I saw. Before, RL on language models mostly meant RLHF, aligning style and preferences. Now the question was whether you could use RL to genuinely push capability, especially on tasks with verifiable outcomes, like whether code runs or a math answer is correct.

Coming from a physics background, what attracted me was that it felt like the early days of a new regime. Nobody had a mature recipe. There were a lot of open problems: how to design environments, how to keep training stable over very long runs, how to stop the model from exploiting the reward instead of learning the real skill. Those are the kinds of problems where I felt I could contribute from first principles rather than just tuning an existing pipeline.

Anthropic in particular felt like a good place for it because they were very serious about coding and agentic use cases, which are exactly where RL with real feedback makes the most sense. And the culture is pretty focused. You don't have a hundred different directions competing; people are fairly aligned on what matters. So my judgment was simple: if RL scaling was going to be the next big thing, I wanted to be in a place where it was a core bet, not a side project.

Looking back, I think the intuition was mostly right, though, honestly, it was a bet at the time. It wasn't obvious it would work as well as it did.

r001.rationale: The response says there was no mature recipe and identifies open problems in designing environments, stabilizing long training runs, and preventing reward exploitation.

r002.rationale: The response describes uncertainty about RL but does not connect it to people not yet having seen o1’s results.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time I wasn't thinking about it as "an opportunity at a company." I was thinking about it as a moment in the field, and the company question came second.

Let me back up a bit. Through most of my PhD, the thing I cared about was language agents, models that act in an environment, take steps, get feedback, and try again. ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, SWE-bench, tau-bench, all of that was circling the same problem. And the frustrating thing was that for years we were doing this on top of models that were trained purely to predict text. We were prompting them into being agents. It worked surprisingly well, but you could feel the ceiling. The model didn't actually learn from the environment. It just had good priors.

So the question I kept asking was, when does the training signal itself come from the environment? When does the loop close? And by the middle of 2024 it was pretty clear to people paying attention that this was starting to happen at scale. Reinforcement learning on reasoning and on tasks with verifiable outcomes was going from a research direction to the main thing frontier labs were betting on. Reasoning models were about to come out. The vibe had shifted from "scale pretraining" to "scale RL."

And when I looked at that, I had a very simple realization. All the problems I had been working on from the outside, how do you build environments, how do you evaluate an agent, what does a good task look like, where does the reward come from, those were no longer side quests. They were the bottleneck. In a pretraining world, data is the internet, and the hard part is compute and infrastructure. In an RL world, data is environments and tasks and rewards, and nobody has that lying around. You have to build it. That's exactly the kind of work I had been doing for five years, except now it was on the critical path of the most important models in the world.

So I understood it as a kind of alignment, in the ordinary sense, between what I had accidentally prepared for and what the field suddenly needed. It's a bit like you spent years learning to make maps for a country nobody visited, and then everyone decides to move there.

The other part is that you can only do certain research inside a lab. Academic RL on language models in 2024 was mostly small models, small environments, and you'd learn things that didn't transfer. The interesting questions, like does RL generalize across tasks, what happens to the model's behavior when you train it to act over long horizons, what breaks in reward design when the model is actually smart enough to exploit you, those only show up at scale. I wanted to be where the questions were real.

I'd say I also had some anxiety about it, to be honest. There's a version of this where you join and you're just a cog in a large pipeline, and the research taste you built doesn't matter. But my read was that in the RL era, taste matters more, not less, because the choices about what to train on are the research. So I decided to go in and see.

r001.rationale: The response describes unresolved questions that only become visible at scale, including RL generalization, long-horizon behavior, and reward design, and says the speaker wanted to work where those questions were real.

r002.rationale: The response says reasoning models were about to come out, but does not attribute widespread uncertainty about large-scale RL to people not yet having seen o1’s results.

astra-6.text:
The way I understood the opportunity was that language models had become strong enough that reinforcement learning could start to do something much more interesting. You weren’t just teaching a model to produce an answer that people preferred; you could potentially teach it to work through a problem, interact with an environment, and improve based on whether it actually succeeded.

That creates a different research question: what do you scale? More compute is part of it, but you also need useful tasks, reliable feedback, and environments where the model can learn something that generalizes. For an agent, even defining success and assigning credit across a sequence of actions can be difficult.

So the attraction, as I understood it, was the combination of a very ambitious direction and a lot of unanswered questions. At a place like Anthropic, the opportunity would be to investigate those questions at a scale where you could actually test whether the ideas worked. That was the exciting part to me: connecting research about learning and agents with the possibility of substantially improving a model’s capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response describes the opportunity as investigating unanswered questions about scaling reinforcement learning and testing ideas at Anthropic.

r002.rationale: It does not mention o1’s results or connect uncertainty about large-scale reinforcement learning to people not yet having seen them.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I understood the opportunity was: pretraining gives you a very capable starting point, but reinforcement learning could let that model improve through actually trying things and getting feedback. That seemed especially important for agents, where you care about whether a sequence of actions accomplishes a task, rather than whether one response looks good.

So the interesting question was whether we could make that learning process work at scale. You need tasks, environments, and feedback you can trust. You also need to know that the model is learning something useful, rather than just exploiting the reward. To me, that combination of research questions and systems challenges was what made the opportunity compelling.

r001.rationale: The response frames making reinforcement learning work at scale as an open question and calls the opportunity a combination of research questions and systems challenges.

r002.rationale: It does not mention widespread uncertainty or connect it to people not yet having seen o1’s results.
